title: Sex-specific inbreeding depression of the life-history traits in Frankliniella occidentalis
content:
Abstract
Inbreeding depression decreases the fitness of progeny resulting from mating between related individuals. The sex-specific response to inbreeding remains unknown in haplodiploid organisms, which have haploid males and diploid females. This research examines the consequences of inbreeding using 2 different inbreeding protocols: full-sib (brother–sister, BS) and maternal backcross (mother–son, MS) on life history, demographic variables, growth in population size, and morphological stability in Frankliniella occidentalis. The experiment was tested for 3 generations: 1 outbred (F1) and 2 inbred (F2 and F3) for both the BS and MS inbreeding regimes. Sibling mating reduced lifetime reproductive productivity from 101.00 to 60.72 (39.9% reduction); maternal backcrossing led to an even greater reduction from 100.20 to 39.10 (61.3% reduction) by F3 generation. Second-clutch egg number declined from 35.42 (control) to 17.85 (BS F3) and 6.45 (MS F3), representing 49.6% and 81.8% reductions, respectively. Net reproductive rate (R0) was reduced from 48.52 to 14.15 (sibling) and to catastrophic levels of 4.85 (backcross; 90.0% reduction). Intrinsic rate of increase (r) was sharply reduced from 0.185 d−1 to 0.088 d−1 (sibling) and 0.024 d−1 (backcross; 87.0% reduction), while the finite rate of increase (λ) declined from 1.203 to 1.092 and 1.024, respectively. Mean generation time (T) increased from 21.05 to 30.12 d (sibling) and 34.60 d (backcross; 64.3% increase). In the case of maternal backcrossing, there was no purging of deleterious alleles in males due to the haploid phase, since their survival rate dropped drastically to 41.4% and malformation levels reached 32.2% overall, with nearly equal distribution between sexes (16.2% in females and 16.0% in males).
